title: Mountain Lions Make Roads Safer
gist: A Current Biology study led by Conservation Science Partners finds that puma presence made wildlife-vehicle collisions significantly less likely on Washington State's Olympic Peninsula, where black-tailed deer caused 92 percent of such collisions from July 2020 to June 2025 — inverting the usual framing of large carnivores as a pure human-safety cost.

insights.claim: The presence of pumas made wildlife-vehicle collisions significantly less likely on Washington State's Olympic Peninsula, meaning a large carnivore functions as de facto road-safety infrastructure.
insights.speaker: Devin Reese
insights.so_what: Carnivore recovery can be argued on transport-safety cost-benefit grounds, not just biodiversity — a materially different funding and permitting case.
insights.locator: A collaboration of biologists, led by Conservation Science Partners

insights.claim: The proposed mechanism is behavioral rather than numerical: carnivores change where prey go and how prey behave, which is what reduces collisions.
insights.speaker: Devin Reese
insights.so_what: A behavior-mediated effect can appear fast and at low predator density — the intervention does not require restoring historical population sizes.
insights.quote: “Carnivores can make roadways safer through their effects on prey behavior and space use,”
insights.locator: explained lead author Justin Suraci in a press release

insights.claim: Black-tailed deer accounted for 92 percent of wildlife-vehicle collisions on the Olympic Peninsula from July 2020 to June 2025, including two human deaths and more than 80 injuries — the harm is concentrated in a single prey species.
insights.speaker: Devin Reese
insights.so_what: A single-species concentration means any lever that shifts deer behavior captures nearly the whole safety benefit.

insights.claim: The wide geographic variation in collision locations across the peninsula — not a uniform rate — is what prompted researchers to test puma presence as the explanatory variable, since black-tailed deer are pumas' primary regional prey.
insights.speaker: Devin Reese
insights.so_what: Spatial heterogeneity is the signal that a local ecological factor, not traffic volume alone, drives collision risk — useful for targeting mitigation spend.

insights.claim: Mountain lions were eliminated from the eastern United States largely because of human fear, even though they predictably avoid places with lots of people — a case where perceived risk drove an irreversible policy outcome that measured risk does not support.
insights.speaker: Devin Reese
insights.so_what: A clean template for fear-driven mispricing of a risk; the same asymmetry shows up wherever vivid low-frequency hazards crowd out diffuse high-frequency ones.
insights.quote: Mountain lions were eliminated from the eastern United States in large part because of our fear of them.

insights.claim: The study was produced by a collaboration led by Conservation Science Partners in California that included experts from several western Native American tribes, showing tribal co-authorship becoming standard in western US carnivore science.
insights.speaker: Devin Reese
insights.so_what: Tribal co-production shifts who holds standing in land and wildlife management decisions across the western US.
insights.locator: A collaboration of biologists, led by Conservation Science Partners
